title: Predictive Policing and the Politics of Patterns
geography: Norway, Germany, Switzerland, Europe, United States, Australia
thesis: Patterns are the epistemological core of predictive policing, but they vary in rationalities and conceal assumptions, making them political.
theme_1_justification: Not addressed. The paper does not discuss dual-use, technology transfer, or the economic properties of software/data.
theme_2_justification: Central argument. The paper extensively discusses the epistemological authority of patterns, algorithmic opacity, black-boxing (proprietary software), and how patterns conceal assumptions and decisions, rendering policing decisions opaque.
theme_3_justification: Substantive engagement. The paper discusses predictive policing as a mode of data-driven governance, algorithmic sorting, and how patterns guide police action and shape understandings of crime, though not explicitly conceptualizing the city as a machinic assemblage.
theme_4_justification: Tangential mention. The paper discusses spatial patterns (hotspots, near-repeat) and potential stigmatization of neighborhoods, but does not address spatial destruction, domicide, or weaponization of urban space.
key_quotes: Patterns are the epistemological core of predictive policing. With the move towards digital prediction tools, the authority of the pattern is rearticulated and reinforced in police work.
The clean surface of the pattern makes it impossible to defend oneself against their results.
Unless patterns are accompanied and contextualized by explanatory material, they render policing decisions opaque.
policy_relevance: The paper calls for greater transparency and reflection on pattern-based policing, suggesting that patterns should be accompanied by explanatory material to allow police officers and affected citizens to interrogate the assumptions behind predictions.
